title: Effect of Camera Angle on Perception of Trust and Attractiveness
key_findings: 12 actors filmed in frontal head-and-shoulder close-ups at 1 m, camera ~30 deg above, at, or ~30 deg below eye level; N=34 viewers (Empirical Studies of the Arts 36, online 2017).
Trust was highest at eye level (M=5.03) vs low angle (M=4.27, p=.007) and high angle (M=4.57, p=.082); low and high did not differ from each other.
No effect of camera angle on attractiveness or on Big-Five personality ratings.

Literature review: earlier findings are heterogeneous (Tiemens 1970 one of three newsreaders; Avery & Long 1976 minor; McCain et al. 1977 higher camera -> higher competence/composure/sociability; Kraft 1987 low=strength, eye=parity, high=weakness; Sevenants 2006 low->potency; Mandell & Shaw 1973 potency; Meridian 1987 no effect).
Authors conclude context and narrative strongly moderate camera-angle effects; Figure 1 lists angles used in prior studies (9-40 deg).
practical_applications: Direct-to-camera trust lines (shop staff, explainer VO with a face) -> eye level by default.
Do not assume low angle = more persuasive for a single talking face.
limitations: Small N (34), students, one context (game-show trust task), 30 deg only.
Large-effect power only (eta_p^2 >= .14).

title: Does it matter to be pictured from below?
key_findings: Three 5-picture stories; the two characters were introduced in high-angle, eye-level or low-angle shots (~35 deg off eye level); linear vs random picture order.
In linear (story) order, low-angle shots raised Potency ratings; no effect on Evaluation or Activation.
In the chess story, the character shown from below was more often chosen as the winner.
In random order (no narrative) no camera-angle effect appeared, contrary to Kraft's (1987) prediction that weaker narrative = stronger angle effect.

Review section: Meyers-Levy & Peracchio (1992) found low angle best for products only under low processing motivation; eye level best under moderate; no effect under high motivation; Meridian (1987) found no effect.
practical_applications: Use low angle on a character only where the story already frames them as the winner/strong one; it reinforces rather than creates meaning.
limitations: Student sample, still pictures, three stories; potency only.
license: open access journal (licence not stated on PDF)

title: The Power of Pictures: Vertical Picture Angles in Power Pictures
authors: Steffen R. Giessner; Michelle K. Ryan; Thomas W. Schubert; Niels van Quaquebeke
key_findings: Four archival studies (six samples) found media tend to depict powerful people from below more than powerless people; a salient power context strengthens this; two experiments found the same for people producing media content.
Explains the verticality-power link with evolutionary (height = formidability), social learning (children look up at powerful parents) and embodiment accounts.
Cites Mignault & Chaudhuri (2003) and Kraft (1987) as evidence that vertical angle shifts dominance judgments.
practical_applications: Picture makers already encode power with vertical angle, so audiences have learned the code; it is a convention reinforced by use.
limitations: Only abstract and introduction (pp. 1-4 of the preprint) read; archival design shows producer behaviour, not viewer effect.

title: The influence of camera angle on comprehension and retention of pictorial events
key_findings: As summarised by Baranowski & Hecht (2018) and Sevenants & d'Ydewalle (2006): slide stories with characters shown from low, eye-level and high (up to ~40 deg) angles; low angles produced impressions of strength, action and superiority, eye level parity, high angles weakness, passivity and insignificance; effects on Potency and Activation, not Evaluation.
Kraft predicted that camera-angle effects grow when narrative structure is weak (later contradicted by Sevenants & d'Ydewalle 2006).
practical_applications: Classic citation for the power reading of vertical angle; use with the replication caveats.
limitations: Not read directly; findings only as reported by the two secondary sources.

title: Judging people in the news - unconsciously: Effect of camera angle and bodily activity
authors: Lee M. Mandell; Donald L. Shaw
key_findings: As summarised by Sevenants & d'Ydewalle (2006): a filmed interview with a fictitious appointee, ~12 deg angles; Potency and Activation were higher in low-angle than high-angle conditions; Evaluation did not differ.
practical_applications: Supports a modest potency effect of low angles on a speaking person.
limitations: Not read directly; bibliographic only.

title: The effect of camera angle on source credibility and attraction
authors: Thomas A. McCain; Joseph Chilberg; Jacob Wakshlag
key_findings: As summarised by Baranowski & Hecht (2018): a higher camera angle raised competence, composure and sociability ratings of a TV speaker (opposite to the power convention); credibility was higher when fewer non-eye-level shots were cut in.
practical_applications: For credibility of a speaker, keep most shots at eye level; angle shifts work only sparingly.
limitations: Not read directly.

title: Getting an angle in advertising: The effect of camera angle on product evaluations
key_findings: As summarised by Sevenants & d'Ydewalle (2006): product evaluations were most favourable for low-angle photos and least for high-angle photos only when processing motivation was low; at moderate motivation eye level was best; at high motivation angle had no effect (heuristic-processing account).
A University of Twente thesis (search snippet) reports a failed replication of the need-for-cognition moderation.
practical_applications: Low-angle product hero shots may help fast-scrolling, low-attention viewers; do not expect them to matter to a careful buyer reading specs.
limitations: Not read directly; exact title taken from search results; moderation contested.

title: Some relationships of camera angle to communicator credibility
key_findings: As summarised by Baranowski & Hecht (2018): only one of three newsreaders was rated higher on communicative ability and knowledgeability from a lower vantage point; no difference on authoritative/convincing.
practical_applications: Evidence that angle effects are small and person-dependent.
limitations: Not read directly.

title: A facial-action imposter: How head tilt influences perceptions of dominance from a neutral face
key_findings: Per press release and abstract snippets: five studies, N=1,517; a downward head tilt with forward gaze increased perceived dominance of a neutral face.
Mechanism: tilt creates the illusion of lowered, V-shaped brows (an 'action-unit imposter' for AU4); the eye/brow region is necessary and sufficient.
practical_applications: A camera BELOW a face makes the head read as tilted UP relative to the viewer; a camera slightly ABOVE with the subject looking up into the lens reads as tilted down. Head pose relative to camera can counteract or reverse the expected low-angle 'power' effect (DERIVED).
limitations: Only press summary and abstract fragments read; head tilt is not the same manipulation as camera angle.

title: The many faces of a neutral face: Head tilt and perception of dominance and emotion
key_findings: As cited by Giessner et al. (2011): 3-D modelled faces shown from seven vertical angles; perceived dominance vs submissiveness varied with vertical head/picture angle.
practical_applications: Supports a vertical-angle/dominance link for faces.
limitations: Not read directly; Journal of Nonverbal Behavior 27(2).

title: Facial expression, size, and clutter: Inferences from movie structure to emotion judgments and back
authors: James E. Cutting; Kacie L. Armstrong
key_findings: ~31,000 shots from 24 films (1940-2010): mean shot duration falls from ~8 s for extreme long shots to ~2.5 s for extreme close-ups.
Valence of faces was classified faster when faces were larger (closer scale): ~150 ms faster across scales 1-6 in movie stills; slight rise at ECU.
Clutter magnified the scale effect (~40 ms low clutter vs ~200 ms high clutter); filmmakers hold small-face, cluttered shots longer.
Seven-step shot scale: ELS, LS, MLS, MS, MCU, CU, ECU defined by focal-character size in frame.
practical_applications: Hold wide/cluttered shots longer; close-ups can be short. Emotion beats need the face big and the background clean.
limitations: Happiness/disgust only; reaction time, not felt emotion.

title: Watching More Closely: Shot Scale Affects Film Viewers' Theory of Mind Tendency But Not Ability
key_findings: N=136, animated film 'Father and Daughter'; a SAD close-up of the girl raised spontaneous references to her mental (affective) states vs the long shot (p=.05) and vs a neutral close-up (p=.013).
A neutral close-up did not differ from the long shot; no effect on ToM ability when prompted.
practical_applications: A close-up only adds empathy when the face carries an emotion; a blank close-up is wasted. Relevant to faceless Mint & Tao: the emotional carrier must be posture/props, not a face (DERIVED).
limitations: One film, one emotion, students, animated stimulus; a corrigendum exists.

title: Perspective Distortion from Interpersonal Distance Is an Implicit Visual Cue for Social Judgments of Faces
authors: Ronnie Bryan; Pietro Perona; Ralph Adolphs
key_findings: Faces photographed simultaneously at ~45 cm vs ~135 cm (and 54 vs 120 cm outdoors), normalised for size, expression and lighting.
Close photos lowered trust-game investment and ratings of trustworthiness, competence and attractiveness (pooled trust d=0.24; effects d=0.14-0.36).
Close faces: nose relatively larger, ears smaller, narrower width-to-height ratio; participants did not notice the manipulation; explicit distance info did not change ratings.
Lens distortion was checked and negligible: the effect is camera DISTANCE (perspective), not lens aberration.
practical_applications: Shoot faces wearing glasses from >= ~1.2-1.5 m (longer lens), never arm's-length wide-angle, for trust and attractiveness.
limitations: 18 base faces, white males; online studies uncontrolled; small effects; ratings intercorrelated.

title: The perceptual basis of common photographic practice
authors: Emily A. Cooper; Elise A. Piazza; Martin S. Banks
key_findings: A picture is correct only from its centre of projection (COP); viewers do not compensate for wrong viewing distance: COP nearer than viewing distance -> depth looks expanded; farther -> compressed.

Preferred viewing distance barely depends on focal length (+20% vs +614% needed to match COP) and mostly on print size; intercept ~25 cm; preferred field of view ~22 deg (small prints) to ~36 deg (large).
Explains the 50 mm 'normal lens' rule (focal length ~ format diagonal, 43.3 mm for 35 mm); median of 3,930 Flickr SLR photos = 68 mm.
Recommends LONGER focal lengths for small images viewed close, e.g. phones (~30 cm).
practical_applications: For phone-viewed IG/TikTok, natural-looking people/products favour short-tele looks (~70-100 mm equiv.) more than 24-35 mm (DERIVED from their recommendation).
limitations: Small N in psychophysics (5-19); equations shown as images on PMC.

title: Why pictures look right when viewed from the wrong place
authors: Dhanraj Vishwanath; Ahna R. Girshick; Martin S. Banks
key_findings: Per abstract: perceived shapes in pictures stay nearly invariant over a wide range of oblique viewing angles when binocular cues to the picture surface are available.
Invariance comes from estimating the local surface orientation of the picture, not from geometric information in the picture; the model also explains perceived distortions in wide-angle pictures.
practical_applications: Off-axis phone viewing is mostly tolerated; wide-angle edge distortion is not cured by this compensation.
limitations: Abstract-level access only.

title: The Arrow in the Eye (online book; chapters V 'The Robustness of Perspective' and VIII 'Marginal Distortions')
key_findings: Extends registry record Kubovy1986 (bibliographic). Robustness of perspective: viewed away from the centre of projection a picture should look sheared/magnified, yet viewers rarely notice; contested, with Rosinski & Farber arguing introspection is not evidence.
Leonardo expected pictures to look wrong unless seen from the COP or from >= 20x the largest dimension of the depicted objects.

Marginal distortion: correctly projected off-axis spheres become ellipses and off-axis columns become wider; painters drew spheres as circles and columns at equal widths, giving each its own principal ray; Uccello's Hawkwood mixes viewpoints.
practical_applications: In wide images, draw/accept round things (lenses, heads, plates) as near-circles near the edges; keep key products near the centre.
limitations: Online book; original publisher/year of this version not stated on pages read; relation to the 1986 Cambridge UP book assumed from authorship.

title: Background Surface and Horizon Effects in the Perception of Relative Size and Distance
key_findings: Describes Sedgwick's (1973) horizon ratio: the horizon cuts objects on the same ground at the observer's eye height, so object size can be read as a multiple of eye height without knowing distance; Rogers (1996) found it works with explicit or implicit horizons in pictures.
Equal projected objects below the horizon: the higher one looks larger; this reverses when the lower object is on/above the horizon; holds for photographs.
The perceived horizon is pulled toward the visible end of the ground surface; distance judgments track height in the image.
practical_applications: Basis of the 'heads on horizon' check for AI images; a visible ground edge (floor/sea line) acts as the horizon for viewers.
limitations: Lab stimuli; size judgments not absolute.

title: The visible horizon: A potential source of visual information for the perception of size and distance (doctoral dissertation)
key_findings: As summarised by Ozkan & Braunstein (2010): objects of equal height are cut by the horizon in the same proportion regardless of distance (horizon ratio).
practical_applications: Geometric rule behind the figure-height check.
limitations: Not read; title as commonly cited, not confirmed this session (dissertation, Cornell).

title: Perspective Made Easy: a step-by-step method for learning the basis of drawing
key_findings: Horizon = eye level wherever you are; objects above it are seen from below, below it from above.

Figure-height transfer: line from a new spot through the feet of a known figure to the eye-level line, then back through the head gives the new figure's height (works whether heads are above or below eye level).
Vanishing points placed close together give 'violent', warped perspective (squares look like diamonds); place them far apart.
Circle in perspective = ellipse; the short (minor) axis lies along the cylinder's centre line (axle), the long axis forms a T with it.
Inclined planes vanish above/below the normal VP on a vertical through it (uphill street above the eye level, roofs on a vertical line).
Parallel edges cast parallel shadows to the same VP on a flat surface; sunlight = parallel rays, a nearby lamp fans shadows.
Reflections: upside down, as far below the surface as the object is above, share the object's VPs.
practical_applications: Source for the drawing procedures in PERSPECTIVE_MASTERY.md and the error library.
limitations: Text read via archive.org OCR (first ~100k characters); craft textbook, not perception research.
license: unknown (1939 US edition; Dover reprint copyrighted)

title: How to Draw: Drawing and Sketching Objects and Environments from Your Imagination
key_findings: Library records: Design Studio Press, 208 pp.; early chapters teach accurate perspective grids and ellipses (incl. 'drawing an ellipse on the minor axis') as the base for complex forms.
practical_applications: Standard reference for grids, minor-axis ellipses, environments.
limitations: Contents only from catalogue records; book text not read.

title: ART 110 Week 2: Perspective Theory - Cone of Vision
authors: Brigham Young University-Idaho, Department of Art
key_findings: Cone of vision drawn as 60 deg from the station point (30 deg each side of the line of sight); objects drawn outside it become distorted.
Placing VP1/VP2 on a small format limits the cone of vision.
practical_applications: Teaching convention for the 60 deg cone.
limitations: States that objects outside the cone 'appear blurred' - a simplification; the drawing distortion is geometric (marginal distortion), not optical blur.

title: Perspective (In)consistency of Paint by Text
key_findings: Forensic geometry checks on DALL-E 2 images (~25 per prompt set): vanishing points of parallel lines, shadow-to-object lines meeting at the light's projection, object-to-reflection lines converging.
Kitchen floors had consistent VPs but countertops did not share the floor's VP/vanishing line in all 25 images: locally consistent, globally inconsistent.
All 25 sunny-day cube images had cast shadows inconsistent with one light; reflections failed in 22 of 25 and even plausible ones failed the geometric test.
practical_applications: Exact procedure for our AI-image perspective/shadow/reflection QC.
limitations: Preprint, one model (DALL-E 2), small exploratory sample; newer models may do better.

title: PreciseCam: Precise Camera Control for Text-to-Image Generation
authors: Edurne Bernal-Berdun; Ana Serrano; Belen Masia; Matheus Gadelha; Yannick Hold-Geoffroy; Xin Sun; Diego Gutierrez
key_findings: T2I outputs often default to a flat camera parallel to the ground with the horizon mid-frame.
Prompt words ('shot from below', 'wide angle', Firefly camera tags) give only coarse control; SDXL could not reproduce lens distortion via prompts at all.
Controls roll, pitch, vertical FOV and distortion with a trained conditioning module (57,380-image dataset).
practical_applications: Expect FLUX/Codex to drift toward eye-level, mid-horizon framing; state angle strongly and verify.
limitations: Preprint; camera accuracy shown mostly qualitatively; SDXL backbone, not FLUX.

title: FLUX.2 prompting guide
key_findings: Extends registry record web:docs.bfl.ai:13. Recommends naming camera, lens and film stock for photorealism ('Shot on Hasselblad X2D, 80mm lens, f/2.8'); JSON schema has camera.angle, camera.distance, camera.depth_of_field.
FLUX.2 does not support negative prompts; write 'sharp focus throughout' instead of 'no blur'.
No dedicated perspective guidance.
practical_applications: Use positive camera phrasing; our local model is FLUX.1 schnell, so treat FLUX.2 advice as a hint.
limitations: Vendor docs for FLUX.2, not schnell; no evidence on how precisely numbers are followed.

title: Gpt-image-1.5 Prompting Guide (OpenAI Cookbook)
key_findings: Camera/composition terms (lens, aperture feel, lighting) steer realism more reliably than generic quality words.
Specify framing/viewpoint (close-up, wide, top-down) and perspective/angle (eye-level, low-angle).
For edits: 'preserve the exact layout, proportions, and perspective'; for composites match lighting, perspective, scale and shadows; re-specify details that drift.
Page marked archived; no stated limits for camera control.
practical_applications: Codex prompt wording for angle/lens; keep the real frame photo via -i and state 'preserve proportions and perspective'.
limitations: Vendor guidance, not tested; model version may differ from what Codex uses.

title: Angle of view (photography)
key_findings: Rectilinear lens focused at infinity: alpha = 2 arctan(d / 2f), d = sensor dimension (36 x 24 mm, diagonal 43.3 mm for full frame).
Close focus: use effective focal length F(1+m); with pupil ratio P: alpha = 2 arctan(d / (2F(1+m/P))).
Defines normal lenses as 36-60 mm on 35 mm format (62-40 deg).
practical_applications: FOV table in LENS_OPTICS.md (recomputed by us).
limitations: Community-edited; its table lists 102.7 deg horizontal for 14 mm while the formula gives 104.3 deg - we use the formula.

title: Hyperfocal distance
key_findings: Extends registry record web:en.wikipedia.org:6. H = f^2/(Nc) + f (approx. f^2/(Nc)); focused at H, sharp from H/2 to infinity; example 50 mm f/8 c=0.03 mm -> H ~ 10.5 m.
Historical sources: Kingslake 1951, Derr 1906, Sutton & Dawson 1867, Taylor 1892.
practical_applications: Deep-focus establishing shots, hyperfocal table.
limitations: Community-edited; formulas cross-checked by our own computation.

title: Depth of field
key_findings: DOF ~ 2u^2Nc/f^2 = 2Nc(1 - 1/M_T)^2 (paraxial approximation, u >> f).
Consecutive depths: focus at H -> H/2..inf; at H/2 -> H/3..H.
Same subject size + same f-number -> almost the same DOF regardless of focal length, but background blur differs.
Diffraction limits sharpness at small apertures, mostly relevant in close-up work; background blur disk b = d m_s x_d / D.
practical_applications: DOF reasoning for eyewear close-ups and AI prompt wording.
limitations: Community-edited; macro formula not given there.

title: Depth of focus
key_findings: Depth of focus = tolerance of the sensor/film position (image side); t = 2Nc(1+m), ~2Nc at low magnification; measured in fractions of a mm.
Depth of field depends on focus distance; depth of focus does not; the terms are often confused. Cites Ray (2000) Manual of Photography.
practical_applications: Vocabulary hygiene: never write 'depth of focus' in a prompt when depth of field is meant.
limitations: Community-edited.

title: Depth of Field and Bokeh
authors: H. H. Nasse (Carl Zeiss Camera Lens Division)
key_findings: Image-side depth of focus depends only on the f-number, not focal length.
Object-side DOF is (almost) independent of focal length at the same imaging scale (subject size), because a longer lens is used from proportionally farther away.
This breaks down at large distances, and the maximum blur of a distant background is LOWER for shorter focal lengths than for longer ones even at equal DOF.
Uses circle of confusion z = 0.029 mm = format diagonal/1500 for 24x36; choice of focal length is decided by room, intended perspective and background.
practical_applications: To melt a shop background behind glasses: longer lens from farther away at the same framing, not just a wider aperture.
limitations: Manufacturer white paper; read in part (pp. 1-10 of ~45).

title: Shutter Angles & Creative Control (RED 101)
key_findings: Shutter angle expresses exposure time relative to frame rate (rotary-shutter origin); 180 deg at 24 fps ~ 1/48 s is the common cinema setting.
Smaller angles (e.g. 45 deg) look stuttered/crisp like 1950s newsreels or modern action; larger angles smear motion more and give more light; 360 deg is the limit.
practical_applications: Motion-blur vocabulary for video prompts and for our rig.js motion blur choices.
limitations: Manufacturer tutorial; formula inferred from the worked example.

title: Distortion (optics)
key_findings: Distortion = deviation from rectilinear projection; changes shape without necessarily reducing sharpness.
Barrel (magnification decreases off-axis; wide-angle, fisheye, wide end of zooms), pincushion (increases; older/cheap teles, binoculars), mustache (barrel centre, pincushion edges).
Brown-Conrady radial model with K1, K2 (negative K1 ~ barrel) and tangential terms; corrected with lens profiles (Lightroom, Lensfun, OpenCV).
Perspective distortion is a separate effect: it does not bend straight lines.
practical_applications: Distinguish bent lines (lens) from big noses/converging verticals (position).
limitations: Community-edited.

title: Perspective distortion
key_findings: Linear perspective changes are caused by distance, not by the lens per se; extension (wide/close) vs compression (tele/far) distortion.
85-135 mm on 35 mm format are generally considered good portrait lenses; viewing a wide image closer (or tele image farther) reduces apparent distortion.
practical_applications: Supports 'distance first, lens second'.
limitations: Community-edited; viewing-distance claim marked citation needed there (but supported by Cooper et al. 2012).

title: Vignetting
key_findings: Types: mechanical (hoods/filters), optical (cured by stopping down 2-3 stops), natural cos^4 falloff (not cured by stopping down; ~56% at 30 deg), pixel vignetting.
Cites Ray (2002) Applied Photographic Optics; artistic use to hold the eye centrally.
practical_applications: Subtle vignette in grade keeps eyes on the product; heavy vignette reads 'toy camera/retro'.
limitations: Community-edited.

title: Chromatic aberration
key_findings: Longitudinal (axial) CA: colours focus at different distances; purple/green fringes in out-of-focus areas; reduced by stopping down; typical of long focal lengths.
Lateral (transverse) CA: magnification varies with wavelength; fringes toward edges; not reduced by stopping down; correctable in software by rescaling channels; typical of short focal lengths.
Corrected by achromats (f1V1 + f2V2 = 0), apochromats, low-dispersion glass, diffractive elements.
practical_applications: Detect fringes on metal frame edges in product photos; add only as a deliberate 'vintage lens' cue.
limitations: Community-edited; no discussion of artistic use.

title: Fisheye lens
key_findings: Mapping functions: rectilinear r = f tan(theta); stereographic r = 2f tan(theta/2); equidistant r = f theta; equisolid r = 2f sin(theta/2); orthographic r = f sin(theta).
Circular fisheye (image circle inside frame, black corners; ~8-10 mm on full frame) vs diagonal/full-frame fisheye (12-18 mm).
Uses: action sports, music videos, peepholes, security cameras, domes/VR.
practical_applications: Peephole/door-camera POV look for story clips.
limitations: Community-edited.

title: Forced perspective
key_findings: Uses angular size/relative size to make objects look larger/smaller/closer/farther; LOTR hobbits (moving sets), Hagrid (scaled props), Potemkin Stairs, Disney castles.
Requirements: enough DOF for both planes, matched lighting/contrast (counter aerial perspective), fixed camera at the zero-parallax point - parallax reveals the trick.
practical_applications: Giant-glasses or tiny-character gags in promo shots and puppet clips.
limitations: Community-edited; cites Purves & Lotto 2003, O'Shea et al. 1994, Mather 1996.

title: Reverse perspective
key_findings: Also inverse/Byzantine perspective: farther objects drawn larger, parallels diverge, vanishing points appear in front of the picture; Byzantine and Russian icons, pre-Renaissance art, Cubism, children's drawings.
Why it arose is still debated.
practical_applications: Deliberate naive/folk look; recognise it as an error when unintended.
limitations: Community-edited.

title: Parallel projection
key_findings: Orthographic (rays perpendicular to the plane) vs oblique (rays at another angle; cavalier, cabinet, military types); axonometric includes isometric, dimetric, trimetric.
Parallel lines stay parallel; length ratios along parallels preserved; circles not parallel to the plane become ellipses; no size change with distance.
Cites Krikke (2000) 'Axonometry: A Matter of Perspective', IEEE CG&A; Carlbom & Paciorek (1978).
practical_applications: Isometric infographics of a shop layout; orthographic front/side views for frame spec sheets.
limitations: Community-edited; isometric 30/120 deg and cabinet half-depth not stated on the page (standard drafting convention, flagged DERIVED/CRAFT in our text).

title: La perspective curviligne (English: Curvilinear Perspective: From Visual Space to the Constructed Image, UC Press 1987)
key_findings: Per Wikipedia (search summary): formally codified curvilinear (five-point) perspective: four VPs around a circle (N, S, E, W) plus one at the centre; straight lines curve as in a fisheye; influenced by Escher; van Eyck's Arnolfini Portrait cited as an early approximation.
practical_applications: Fisheye/POV panels in carousels and clips.
limitations: Book not read; details from a Wikipedia search summary.

title: Using Blur to Affect Perceived Distance and Size
authors: Robin T. Held; Emily A. Cooper; James F. O'Brien; Martin S. Banks
key_findings: Probabilistic model of how viewers combine defocus blur with other pictorial cues to estimate absolute distance and hence scale; an algorithm adds blur to sharp images to change perceived distance/size (the link to the tilt-shift miniature look is OUR reading; the paper does not use that term) (effect).
Experiment agreed closely with the model; some common blur approximations worked and others did not.
practical_applications: Miniature/diorama look: strong blur gradient consistent with the scene's depth = small scale; inconsistent blur bands fail (DERIVED).
limitations: Abstract only (ACM TOG 29(2), article 19).
Spot-check 2026-11-25: original wording checked; finding corrected to match the source.

title: Contrast as a depth cue
authors: Robert P. O'Shea; Shane G. Blackburn; Hiroshi Ono
key_findings: Per abstract/secondary citations: the lower-contrast region was judged farther, monocularly and binocularly, even when size pointed the other way; contrast acts as a pictorial cue mimicking aerial perspective.
Follow-up O'Shea, Govan & Sekuler (1997, Perception): blur is a depth cue independent of contrast.
practical_applications: Lower contrast/raise value of backgrounds to push them back; keep the product at highest contrast.
limitations: Abstract/search-summary level only.

title: Shot (filmmaking)
key_findings: Field sizes: extreme long, long/wide (often establishing), full, medium long (frame ends near the knees), American/cowboy (upper thighs, holster), medium (around the waist), MCU (more shoulder), CU (shoulder line visible), ECU (chin to forehead or a detail), Italian shot (eyes only), two shot.
Reverse shot = 180 deg turn to the previous image, often with POV/OTS; insert replaces the picture while audio continues.
Cites Bowen 'Grammar of the Shot' 4th ed. 2018, Katz 'Film Directing Shot by Shot' 1991, Ascher & Pincus 1999.
practical_applications: Shared shot-size vocabulary in CAMERA_ANGLE_LIBRARY.json.
limitations: Community-edited; definitions vary across textbooks.

title: Ultimate Guide to Camera Shots
key_findings: Practitioner taxonomy: EWS, WS, FS, MWS (knees up), cowboy (mid-thighs up, from Westerns), MS, MCU (chest up), CU, ECU; single/dirty single, two/three shot, OTS, over-the-hip, POV; eye/low/high/hip/knee/ground/shoulder level, Dutch, bird's eye/overhead (treated as one), aerial.
Stated purposes (craft): EWS isolation/unfamiliarity, low angle power, high angle inferiority, Dutch disorientation, ground level shows what the subject stands on.
practical_applications: Naming conventions for shot lists.
limitations: Craft claims, no evidence; treats overhead and bird's eye as identical.

title: Cutaway (filmmaking)
key_findings: A cutaway interrupts continuous action with a view of something else, usually returning to the original shot; used to adjust pace, hide removed material, join two takes; documentary 'noddies' cover cuts; cites Brown (2012) Cinematography: Theory and Practice.
practical_applications: Cover jump cuts in staff/VO clips with shop-detail cutaways.
limitations: Community-edited; insert vs cutaway not distinguished there.

title: Film Art: An Introduction (9th ed.)
key_findings: Cited by Sevenants & d'Ydewalle (2006, citing the 2004 edition) for the practice of distinguishing mainly three vertical camera positions - high, eye level, low - out of an infinite number of possible angles, and by Baranowski & Hecht (2018, 9th ed. 2010) for the conventional readings (low = dominance, high = vulnerability, eye level for neutral/factual).
practical_applications: Canonical vocabulary reference.
limitations: Not read this session; cited only via the two papers.
